cells.speakerNotes: Welcome! We're really excited to be here today.

I'm Tobias, and this is my co-presenter Gerald.

We're both employee-owners of Caktus Group, a small Django development company based in North Carolina.

I'm a developer and devops person, and Gerald leads quality assurance for Caktus.

We had a lot of help with this presentation from our colleagues Colin and Simon, who helped with working out the slides and the initial implementation for our client, respectively.

To set the stage today, we need to take a step back and talk about criminal record expungement.

(Tobias) For this section of the presentation I will hand it off to Gerald.

(Gerald) This is an area of legal aid where non-profit organizations, public defenders,
and sometimes private attorneys help community members clear eligible charges
from their records, such as dismissed or not guilty charges.

For someone trying to secure housing or apply for a job, an expungement can
be life-changing. But under the hood, the process of preparing these petitions
is painfully manual. Attorneys and paralegals must manually track down potentially
hundreds of records of a period of decades, verify every single charge, and
transcribe everything onto strictly formatted court forms.

Everything starts with intake. A client comes in, and staff need to
collect every name they've gone by, their date of birth, and the counties they've lived in, so nothing gets missed in the search that
follows.

This is the step we're focused on today. Staff then have to search court and
law-enforcement databases for every record tied to that client, and
names are sometimes typed inconsistently — misspellings, nicknames, abbreviations —
so a simple exact-match search misses records.

Once every record is found, each charge gets checked against state
statutes to see if it qualifies for expungement.

From there, every eligible charge has to be transcribed onto strictly
formatted court petition forms, by hand — another
manual, error-prone step in this process.

Finally, the completed petition is filed with the court. If it's
granted, the records are cleared — but getting here can take weeks of
manual work for a single client.

When we first took on this project, our assumption was that the core
challenge would be eligibility mapping, PDF form generation or other aspects of the
workflow—taking client data, applying NC statute rules, and cleanly
injecting it into standardized court paperwork. But then we held a
dedicated discovery workshop with our client.

During the workshop, we realized that finding the proper records
quickly was the true bottleneck preventing eligible community
members from getting help.

Thorough record checks are critical because conviction expunctions in North Carolina are generally a one-shot opportunity. Once a court grants a conviction expunction, the client cannot use that statute again—meaning any omitted conviction stays on their record permanently. Comprehensive statewide searches are essential due diligence to ensure every eligible charge is included before filing.

Here is the core problem: the state transitioned away from its legacy system
to a "modern" web portal. While you might expect a newer system to speed up
legal workflows, in reality, it severely restricted how attorneys can search
for records.

As you can see on screen, doing a simple name search in this portal routinely
takes 10 to 15 seconds—or longer—per query. In our discovery workshop with the
client, staff shared that under the new portal system, their record-pulling time
grew from 3 hours up to 10 hours per client. To make matters worse, while the
system claims to offer fuzzy search matching, the underlying logic is poorly
implemented, ballooning an 6 item search result to 200+ results when selected.
When enabled, it ends up matching too many false positives, rather than giving attorneys what they actually need.
And because the new system caps the search results at 200 records, the risk of missing records is real.

So why is finding everyone so hard? In our case, we were dealing with a
database of over 50 million North Carolina court records, and searching by
name in a dataset that size is not trivial.

First, we're not just looking for a single record. We're looking for every
record that belongs to a single person.

Second, if you think about the lifespan of a criminal record, one can imagine how
typos are frequent. A name might be typed on the side of the road by an
arresting officer, transcribed from a hand-written form by a busy court clerk,
or supplied by a client who spells their name differently
across various legal documents, uses nicknames, or hyphenated names.

On top of that, name collisions are everywhere—thousands of people share the
exact same first and last name. And date of birth—the one field that could
easily disambiguate two people—is sometimes missing in court data.

We realized that if we wanted to build a tool that truly served legal aid
organizations, public defenders, and community advocates, we had to solve
the multi-million record fuzzy search problem using our tools of choice,
Django and PostgreSQL.

To talk more about that, I'll hand it off to Tobias.

To help understand the scope of the problem and some of the assumptions we as programmers and technologists might make about names, we highly recommend the article linked here, "Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names," by Patrick McKenzie in 2010.

Some of them are pretty funny, and I recommend reading through them all on your own time.

To share just 5 of the 40,

one is that people have exactly one name. In reality, they may have multiple aliases, spellings, nicknames that they use regularly.
Another is that names often change over time, through marriage, divorce, or simply deciding to change one's name.

Another is that people have a different first name and last name --and this hits close to home with Django's User model--that they have a first name and last name at all. In other countries and cultures, names often don't fit into the neat "first name" and "last name" boxes.

Another assumption is that names are written in ASCII.

In our case, the entire database of 54 million plus court records was written in ASCII, so non-ASCII characters were simply not present in our dataset.

Finally--and this one is was also abundant on our project--it's easy to assume that names will be typed exactly and perfectly every time they're entered. This is not the case, and our dataset of 54M records provided ample evidence of this.
